Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Acting Minister. of Finance) moved the second reading of bill No. 373, to amend the Dominion Succession Duty Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Substituted first schedule.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a question in connection with a situation which arises frequently, particularly in respect of smaller estates where an executor designate or an applicant for administration finds it impossible, owing to financial difficulties, to make payment of succession duties even though there are moneys in the bank. I offer to the minister a suggestion which comes from two or three sources. One of these, Mr. H. E. Keown, K.C., is a bencher of the law society of Saskatchewan. If the suggestion made here were adopted it would help materially an executor designate or an applicant for administration. I shall read from the letter, because I feel it sets out the facts more clearly than I could hope to do:
Where there is a bank account the executor, after the application for letters probate or administration have been filed, is unable to issue a cheque until the necessary release is received from the dominion succession duty department. I take the position that succession duty due, either to the dominion or the province, is a first charge against the estate and should be paid.
My practice has been to have the executor or administrator issue a cheque on the bank account payable to the department, forward the cheque to the department asking them to send the necessary release to deposit with the bank and hold the cheque a day or two. However, it usually works out that the release has not been received by the time the cheque comes through and the bank then returns the cheque unpaid, which causes considerable inconvenience.
This gentleman suggests that in order to improve the process of collection of succession duties a change be made, either by amendment to the act or by regulation, whereby an executor or administrator could issue the necessary cheque for payment, either to the dominion or to the province, or to both, notwithstanding the fact that the release had not been received from the respective departments. I do not think there is anything in the suggestion which would interfere with the routine practice, and I believe it would be beneficial to executors designate and applicants for administration.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for his suggestion. It does sound like a matter which could be handled administratively, as he has suggested, without amendment to the law. I am not sufficiently familiar with the practice in the common law provinces to know what is done in connection with an executor designate. But in my own province we often do adopt a practice somewhat similar to the one suggested. We arrange with the provincial succession duties office to take a cheque in payment of succession duties, the cheque being issued on the bank account be-
Customs Tariff

fore complete returns have been filed, and before the general waivers have been issued. The practice there is to give authorization to the bank to pay that cheque. In some cases where preliminary returns can be filed, if it is thought desirable to do so they will even release some other assets.
I am pleased to have my hon. friend's suggestion. My colleague the Minister of National Revenue has followed it closely. The matter will be discussed with departmental officials to see whether or not it would be practicable to arrange the administrative regulations so as to permit what the hon. member has suggested.
Would an estate, part of which is in Maryland and part in Ontario, have to pay four separate succesion duties, namely to the dominion, to Ontario, to Maryland and to the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is possible. The
liability for succession duties depends both upon the situs of the assets and the domicile of the deceased at the time of death. The estate of a man who dies in Ontario would be liable for succession duties on all assets wherever situate, both for dominion and for provincial succession duty purposes. He can take credit for certain duti'es paid abroad, I understand; and my colleague the Minister of National Revenue informs me that under the tax agreement with the United States the estate would be able to take credit for duties paid to the United States, thereby to some extent eliminating double succession duties.
Has an agreement been reached with the old country in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I believe it was approved in the house a few days ago.
Is the minister satisfied with the word "successor", a word which I do not believe is familiar in the common law? Is the word sufficiently defined to be familiar to the courts?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The word "successor" is defined in the interpretation section of the Dominion Succession Duty Act, and I believe has been in the act since it was adopted. I have not given any special consideration from the legal point of view to the question whether the term is or is not appropriate. It is defined in paragraph (n) as follows: "'successor' means the person entitled under a succession." Then the word "succession" is defined at considerable length.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Allowable deductions.

Has any effect been given to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver South on July 26, when the resolutions were being discussed, following which the minister said he would give the matter consideration? I cannot tell offhand from looking at the bill whether consideration has been given to it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I had intended making a statement, but I saw the hon. member for Vancouver South was not in the house. When the resolutions on which this bill is based were before the committee the hon. member for Vancouver South suggested that double rates should apply only in those provinces which consented to give up their succession duties, and that the present rates continue in force in those provinces which had not by agreement given up those duties. At that time I told the hon. member that I would explore his suggestion.
Upon looking into the matter I find that his suggestion was considered prior to the making of the off* to the provinces, but that it could not be adopted since it meant that the dominion law would not be uniform in application in all parts of Canada. I think hon. members will agree it would be highly improper under a dominion statute to levy one set of rates of duties for application in some provinces and a different set of rates for application in others. For this reason it was felt the hon. member's suggestion was not one which could be adopted.
iMr. FULTON: I do not think anyone will disagree with the suggestion that it would be unfair or inadvisable to levy different sets of rates. But could not the matter be taken care of by making a differential in the amount to be deducted? The act as it stands at present allows a successor to deduct from duties otherwise payable either the amount he pays to the provinces or fifty per cent of the duty otherwise payable, which ever is .the lesser. It seems to me a third paragraph could be inserted providing that if the effect of the preceding two paragraphs is that a successor will now have to pay more duty than he would before the act came into force, he shall be allowed to deduct an amount so as to equalize his tax with that paid in the other provinces, or with that previously paid. Then the minister would be applying a uniform rate, and simply varying the amount of deduction.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I do not know whether I am quite right in this, but it seems to me the suggestion the hon. member is putting forward would be that in some provinces a man would be entitled to deduct a fixed amount,

Customs Tariff
say up to fifty per cent of the dominion tax, whether he had paid it to the province or not. It seems to me it is clear that that would result in a person in one province paying a lesser sum than one in another.

I was not referring to the question whether it was paid or not. If the effect of this bill is that the total tax to the successor both dominion and provincial, will be increased, then he should be allowed to make a larger deduction from the amount of the dominion tax than in the other province where the net result is different. In other words, if you had a uniform scale of rates it would simply allow the deductions to follow.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think it would have exactly the effect I indicated a moment ago. If my hon. friend will reduce it to a concrete case I think he will see my point. Assuming that the dominion tax would be $200, the provincial tax would be $100, making a total of $300-[DOT] that is as things stand now. If the dominion is doubling its rates the new dominion tax would be $400 while the tax in the province would still remain at S100. Under the proposed law he would be entitled to deduct from his dominion tax of $400 either the amount he has paid in the province or fifty per cent of the dominion tax, whichever is the lesser. In that case he would deduct $100 and his net dominion tax would be $300, the provincial tax remaining at $100. He would be paying the same tax as the man in another province whose dominion tax was $400.

Section agreed to.
Section 3 agreed to.
On the schedule.

Perhaps the question I intend to ask will show my ignorance of succession duties generally, but I am happy to have that happen if I can obtain an answer. The schedule of rates shown here strikes me as being exceedingly generous to the person who receives an estate. Where a person receives an estate or a sum of money as a result of a bequest is there any tax levied by the federal government in addition to the regular succession duty tax? In the case of a $35,000 estate, a class A beneficiary would pay -a tax of six per cent, which would amount to $2,100; then the rates for other classes of beneficiary go up slightly but none of them seems to be too burdensome when an estate of that magnitude is passed. Is that property or money also subject to some other tax?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
This is a capital amount received as a result of succession. My hon. friend has referred to an estate of $35,000. Such an estate left by a young or middle aged
professional man might represent life insurance being left to his widow. It would represent his savings over a period of years and it is left to his widow and children to help take them over the rest of their lives. That estate would pay the tax indicated here, but the income in the form of dividends or whatever it is *would be subject to income tax from the date of the man's death. The capital levy, if I may call it that, is the succession duty tax which is paid following the death of the deceased.
The minister has taken the most compassionate case; that of an immediate widow.
Take the $5,000,000 one.

I will still stick with this $35,000 estate; that is big enough for me to discuss. I am prepared to concede that there is a case for the widow', but the utter stranger, who would be considered a class D beneficiary, pays only ten per cent, so his capital accretion would be $31,500 net. There would be no further tax on that net amount except as it produces income.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is right. Of course when he dies it goes through the same process again if it is still there.
When we think of an eight per cent sales tax on a number of modest commodity purchases and compare it with a ten per cent tax paid by a class D beneficiary, it does not seem sufficient.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Perhaps a word of explanation would be useful. This bill does three things: it eliminates the flat rate of excess profits tax and incorporates it with the corporation tax, it removes partnerships and sole proprietors from the operation of the Excess Profits Tax Act, and it reduces from 20 to 15 per cent the rate of tax payable on profits in excess of 116% of standard. The other changes are incidental to accomplishing these purposes.

I am not quite sure that I have read this correctly, but unless there is an explanation which does not occur to me, the effect of this section is to do away with the minimum of $5,000 which was incorporated last autumn. What is the reason for that? I am looking now at the act of 1945, section 3, subsection 2.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is no change in substance in the act in that respect. Perhaps there may be some confusion in numbering the section.
What I am referring to is printed in the explanatory notes, at the bottom, opposite the first page.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

(2) The aggregate of the taxes exigible under paragraph two of the first part of the second schedule to this act and under the Income War Tax Act shall in no case operate-

On section 5, which is the substance of the bill, I have on two different occasions made an argument to which the minister-not the acting minister-gave a reply which in my opinion was fallacious, and I quoted both my argument and the minister's contention when the acting minister had the resolutions in front of him. To refresh his memory, I may say that my argument is that the excess profits tax of 15 per cent is very detrimental to business and employment in this country because of the invidious comparison of taxation of business in Canada with taxation in the United States particularly. I do not know whether I need to rehearse the various points with the minister. He may have them in his mind. Succinctly, however, the situation is this. Our tax on business is 30 per cent plus 5 per cent for the provinces, and if your business volume is large, as most businesses are, there is a 15 per cent excess profits tax, making our rate 50 per cent as against the United States rate on larger corporations-it is less on smaller businesses-of 38 per cent. The Minister of Finance, winding up the budget debate, after quoting the figures I had given, made this statement at page 3596:
But taking the tax over the whole range of their business,-
Speaking of Canadians.
t they will have to have very large excess profits indeed for their excess profits tax and their corporation tax to he greater than 38 per cent plus state taxes in the United States.

Then he said:
What therefore becomes of this argument that by our short-sighted, ignorant way of taxing corporations we are going to drive manufacturing business from Canada to the United States?
No answer was given by the acting minister when I contended that the position taken by the Minister of Finance was most fallacious. The minister said, taking the tax over the whole range of their business, there was not an unfair comparison with the American tax. It seemed to me that that was very much like telling the working man who refused to work on Fridays, or more particularly on Saturdays, because he got into a higher bracket, that his average rate was not at all bad, only five or six per cent. That was not what interested the working man. What concerned him was that his tax on Friday or Saturday was 25, 30 or 40 per cent. In the same way, businesses-and I mention particularly American companies that have tremendous investments in branch plants in Canada, amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars-would find, as far as their export business was concerned, that it would be more profitable to do that export business from their American plants where the retainable profit was greater than it was if they did the business from their Canadian branches. The minister's contention that the average rate of profit was the one that determined the question has nothing to do with the matter, as I see it. If our rate is 50 per cent in the taxation of business in the excess profits tax class, whereas in the United States there is no excess profits tax and the rate is 38 per cent, or one or two per cent more, allowing for state tax, if there is any-I have not heard of any-then it will certainly have a deterrent effect on Canadian business. Therefore the provision of this excess profits tax is .to my mind in direct contradiction to many of the government's policies.
The government is spending a great deal of money in advertising through the Department of Trade and Commerce; it has representatives abroad, and there is a great deal of money entailed in the Exports Credits Insurance Act. We are appropriating hundreds of millions, in fact billions, in order to give credits to other countries to buy our goods. We are spending money on the Canadian Commercial Corporation-$10,000,000 I believe-for the purpose of developing our trade, and we have similar items in connection with the Canadian information service, all of which, as part of their purpose, are intended to develop our trade. Yet we find the enterprising manufacturer placed under a competitive handicap, and export business is largely lost to a great

many concerns, particularly where the alternative is to manufacture either in the United States or in Canada. I mentioned a Canadian manufacturer who was developing some business in Newfoundland. He found that he lost out to a United States firm because that firm had more retainable profit and could quote a lower price on the product. Therefore the government is working at cross purposes with itself in keeping this tax and at the same time trying to develop the export business of the country. It indicates to those of us who should approach this subject with an open mind that there is a complete lack of business experience in the Department of Finance or on the part of those who are advising the government on these matters. It also indicates that the present administration do not do as some other Liberal administrations did, namely, consult with business men, even of their own political persuasion, and find out exactly how some of these tax laws would affect business and employment.
At the present time Canada has a wonderful opportunity of developing export business, because so few countries are in the fortunate position, as we are, of being able to offer goods in the export market. But our government does not seek practical advice on these matters and has little or no practical experience in the field; they are muffing the ball. They are nothing but football strategists who never saw a playing field or even a dressing-room, but live in the ivory tower of the clubhouse. I should be pleased if the minister would answer my argument.

I am sorry I was not here on Saturday afternoon when this item was discussed. I understand the hon, member for New Westminster spoke on dred-ing, and I wish to concur in everything he said. So far as the Fraser river is concerned conditions have changed owing to the fact that the surrounding territory is all logged
Supply-Public Works

out. Because of that there is a much quicker run-off of water than used to toe the case years ago. The dredge used out there is thirty or forty years old. It is supposed to take care of the whole Fraser river, including the finest fresh water stretch in the Dominion of Canada, that around New Westminster. The present dredge cannot possibly look after the Westminster area alone, quite apart from the whole Fraser valley. The farmers are in danger because the Department of Public Works are unable to keep the channel open. In addition the vast investment in the Canadian National Railways is endangered because the line may go out at any time owing to the floods. If that happens it will be a serious matter in the Fraser river valley, the New Westminster district and the whole of Canada.
In spite of the fact that the government says it is not the duty of the federal department, I think it is unreasonable to expect the local districts to look after the river banks and erosion. It might have been all right forty years ago to say that it was a local matter; but conditions have changed and each year we are losing a tremendous amount of earth and farms into the river through erosion. Earth and silt are clogging up the channel. I understand that the federal department is responsible for navigation channels. But the act which gave them that authority was drawn many years ago, and conditions in that respect also have changed. The reason we have so much erosion is that the channels are not kept open. In the Fraser river there are many places where sandbars have closed the channels. Years ago boats could cross over these places, but now you can wade across in rubber boots. That should be obvious even to the Department of Public Works.
As far as dredging is concerned, I want to support what was said by the hon, member for New Westminster. The present dredge is entirely inadequate, and it is time the federal department gave an order for a new modern dredge. I understand there is one down in the Columbia district which should serve as an example of the class and size of dredge we need. I want to urge the minister not to wait until the Canadian National is put out of business before something is done. Some years ago the dike at Matsqui broke, and for forty-eight hours the railway was out of action and the city of Vancouver was cut off. We all hope there may never be another war, but suppose that had happened during the war period, when we were rushing supplies not only to Canadian and British forces on the Pacific coast but also to American forces, who as far as that area was concerned received

most of their supplies over the Canadian National. What would have happened if the dike had gone out then? I hope there will be no more wars, though I doubt it very much, but look at it in a broad sense; if that should happen what would be the result? In addition, the city of Vancouver and the people of British Columbia are entitled to some consideration, since Vancouver is our only Pacific port of any importance, and the possibility that it might be cut off is a serious matter to the business men there. My friends of the stock exchange in Toronto talked a long time about $3.20 or something in regard to the gold market. We are entitled to talk about the few industries we have in British Columbia, and surely this government cannot afford to risk the possibility of having those industries cut off and men thrown out of work, when that possibility may be avoided by doing a very little dredging. I am not an engineer, but I think the solution to the problem of erosion, at least, is dredging the channel properly.
Unfortunately I did not hear the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo on Saturday, but I understand he made reference to some filth in the Fraser river. I am glad the hon. member for New Westminster was here; he could be depended upon to do something about it; but the only time water runs uphill, as far as I know, it when the filth from the other side comes up the Fraser river. We have no filth coming down the Fraser river. Not knowing what the hon. member said I cannot very well reply, but I am sure my colleague from New Westminster gave a good answer. Any filth we have in the Fraser river would be going to the proper depository if it went across the channel.

I want to make similar complaints about a much more important river than the Fraser; I refer to the Columbia river that flows from the Big Bend1 country to the north of my constituency, south into the United States. We have had steamer navigation on the river to my knowledge for something over fifty years. In the early years of this century the dominion government undertook an extensive dredging programme to aid navigation between the upper and lower Arrow lakes, and to permit steamers to land at the docks at Arrowhead. In those years we had a very small population, possibly only two or three hundred people in a distance of 150 miles. Later the population grew considerably, and we had an all-year boat service from one end of the lakes to the other. Dredging operations were later curtailed, and to-day, with a greatly increased popula-

Supply-Public Works
tion, with much greater activity in farming and lumbering, we only have through service from about the end' of April until the beginning of November, owing to the fact that the expenditure on dredging has been limited. As a result, at low water steamers cannot go between the upper and lower lakes. I suggest to the minister that he provides a larger appropriation in order to keep open the channel between the upper and lower Arrow lakes, and in addition I should like to draw to his attention the fact that silt from the Columbia entering the upper Arrow lake is deposited in large quantities on bars around the mouth of the river and the wharf at Arrowhead. I suggest to the minister, and I have had this advice from skippers who have operated on the lakes for a number of years, that a considerable portion of the expense of dredging around the wharf at Arrowhead, and possibly a portion of the bar at the mouth of the Columbia river, could be avoided if the department could get the Canadian Pacific to move their dock at Arrowhead some three *hundred yards to the east, where there is deep water, and the area is never silted up.
I do not suggest that we should have a new or larger dredge on the Columbia, because we all realize that within the next few years we may have immense developments in that area which will completely change the situation. But I do ask the minister to give consideration to an increased appropriation for dredging, particularly between the upper and lower Arrow lakes, because when the season is curtailed and we do not have through steamer traffic it is a great handicap and inconvenience to the whole district. I should like to know what is the appropriation for dredging this year.

I have been seeking some item upon which I might bring to the attention of the minister a matter of some importance, and it seems to me that this is the appropriate item. My observations

shall not be directed, to the inclusion in the estimates of a certain sum of money, but rather to a matter which the minister has had before him, and one to which I believe the department feels its jurisdiction does not extend.
Along the shores of lake Ontario, and I fancy the same would apply to the shore lines along others of the great lakes, a considerable degree of erosion has taken place within the last few years. Many newspapers and other publications have carried news items and pictures showing the serious degree to which this erosion has developed in the great lakes area. While there seems to be some difference of opinion as to the cause of this condition, there is a feeling in the Port Credit area, and at points lying along the shore line of Peel county, that it comes from an artificial diversion or change made at points nearer the headwaters. In my part of Ontario this condition of erosion has reached serious proportions. Many of the residents in the south portions of Peel find that those parts of their properties abutting the lake have been worn away, and the foundation of their homes endangered thereby.
I have made an appeal to the minister privately, and received the courteous consideration one would expect from him. I would ask him now however to consider the responsibility of the federal government in respect of this problem. If the experience in other parts of Canada'is similar to that which we have had, the loss must run into many millions of dollars in the great lakes area.
Local authorities have attempted to relieve the situation by various means, but in many cases the projects overreach the financial ability of the municipalities to pay. I would ask the minister to see if the department can do something to help. My only regret is that the minister has not been able to visit that part of Ontario to see what the condition is, because I know if he did see it he would consider it most serious. He knows, of course, that no matter what be the occasion for his visit, he would be a most welcome visitor in that part of the country at any time-as indeed the Minister of Veterans Affairs has been on many occasions. I suggest that departmental officials, and if possible the minister, ought to visit the area to see what is happening, having in mind the possibility of extending the dominion's jurisdiction to relieve the suffering and loss that is now being sustained.

The condition of erosion along lake Ontario, as well as other lakes and rivers in Canada, has become

serious. We are willing to admit that in the Department of Public Works. Speaking generally, two kinds of protection works would be studied by my department, under the first of which we admit responsibility by stating that the erosion has been caused by some works or act of the federal government. In cases of that kind, on both coasts and along the shores of rivers and lakes, we do a considerable amount of protection work. The second type of erosion, which arises from natural causes, and has not arisen from anything done by the federal government, is not generally accepted as a federal problem.
I believe that in 1932 the government did in a general vote, and for the purpose of relieving unemployment in years of depression, spend moneys on this second type of work. The vote, which was originally under the Department of Labour, was transferred to the Department of Public Works, and the result was that in each province we undertook protective works.
I do not believe there is any subject which causes so much correspondence in our department as requests for protection works. The policy of the government is to assume what we believe to be our responsibility, and to do those works. Other works would seem to come more under provincial or municipal authorities. As the hon. member for Peel has said, in some instances the damage is so great that the local authorities cannot meet the needs. I cannot say that at this session, even in the supplementary estimates, I can get an amount for protection works of that kind. As time goes on we are making a serious study in the hope that we shall have an amount of money to relieve the most pressing cases, or to conduct works at points where the most damage has been done by erosion. I would not wish, however, to have people hoping too much that I shall succeed in getting money for that purpose. When we make demands for our estimates we are bound to stay within our jurisdiction, and unless there is a general consensus in the house that the federal government should undertake these works, I should imagine that condition would continue. If we ever did undertake them we would have to spend millions upon millions of dollars on works which up to the present have never been recognized as our responsibility.
I sympathize with the hon. member for Peel and with many other hon. members. Indeed I do not think there are ten members in the house who have not in their own ridings suffered damage from erosion of this kind. If there were a vote for this type of damage, undoubtedly there is not a township along the

I should like to add a word to what has been said by the hon. member for Peel. He is perhaps the first member who has brought before the house something which I predicted years ago was going to happen. I am sorry to say that I fear this government is confronting the necessity of fighting thousands and upon thousands of damage actions through riparian rights which have been or may be destroyed. As my hon. friend has said, erosion has occurred, and I am going to give the minister the cause. You must consider the cause when you start negotiating about these matters. Perhaps the minister will remember that a bill passed this house a few years ago permitting a diversion of water in northern Ontario of 5,200 cubic feet per second from the Albany river watershed to the St. Lawrence river watershed. At that time Chicago had been taking perhaps
10,000	cubic feet per second from lake Michigan, and there was an argument advanced that the levels of the great lakes would be maintained by this diversion from the Albany river watershed to the St. Lawrence river watershed. However, since that time the United States government has had the diversion at Chicago reduced to 1,500 cubic feet per second in accordance with a United States supreme court order. In order to check my figures I wrote to the chief engineer at Chicago a few days ago to inquire what was being taken out of lake Michigan at the present time, and he replied that they were taking 1,500 cubic feet per second.
As I said a moment ago, we are diverting into the St. Lawrence river watershed 5,200 cubic feet per second which God Almighty never intended should go into that watershed. If we deduct the 1,500 cubic feet being taken out at Chicago, we find that an additional
3,700	cubic feet, are pouring into the great lakes watershed every second in the year. The farmers along the whole lake front in Ontario will have a right to sue this government and the Ontario government for any destruction of their property as the result of this diversion. I fear it will not be long until every farmer along the shores of lake Ontario, lake Erie, lake Huron and Georgian Bay, and on the American side as well as on our side, will be suing the governments because of loss of riparian rights. A total of
3.700	cubic feet is pouring into this watershed every second and the water levels have been raised. I looked at the record of the levels this morning, not anticipating that this vote would be discussed, and I find that the general levels in these lakes have risen until they are not far short of the highest average levels before the forests were cut down.
I am afraid that this government and the United States government may be in for a series of headaches because of suits by property owners along the shores of the great lakes. In my judgment they have an absolute claim. In this case man has deliberately peured into the St. Lawrence watershed a vast volume of water from an outside watershed. We are told that it means an increased power production, but if that is so, should those who are producing the power reimburse the farmers fronting on lake Ontario, fronting on lake Erie, and fronting on lake Huron? I am sure the department must have been appalled at the multitude of letters they have received because of the breaking of the dikes in Essex county. I was up to that end of the province this last week-end and I know what the people are thinking. Those dikes were never intended to withstand the level of water that there is now in the summer time.
I do not want to be misunderstood about this. I am quite in accord with water levels being maintained, and I realize that something had to be done when Chicago was taking from 10.000 to 15.000 cubic feet per second; but according to the information I got from Chicago a few days ago, that is no longer being done. As I said before, they are now down to 1,500 cubic feet per second. I think the Department of Public Works should take close notice of what is happening in the great lakes watershed. Every second a total of
3.700	extra cubic feet is being poured into our great lakes. That is bound to be felt along the shores of lake Ontario, lake Erie and lake Huron. It will not affect the shores of lake Superior particularly because there is a dam at Sault Ste. Marie which controls the level of that lake. By raising the gates they are able to let the water out and maintain the lake at a static level, but there is no such control for lake Huron, lake Erie or lake Ontario.
At times there are many advantages in an increased level of water, but to-day, we have had a just presentation made by the hon. member for Peel. I believe the farmers in his county will have a just claim for protection again erosion caused by lake Ontario water being kept at such a high level at certain seasons of the year, a level at which God Almighty never intended it should be kept.

A road extension thirty-five miles in length is being built by the Northern Transportation company, who are to be reimbursed for the amount actually expended. The old section of the road, approximately ten miles and a half in length, requires reconditioning and reconstruction of bridges and culverts thereon. This work was started in 1945; there was an item in the estimates of 1945-46. In 1946-47 we are repairing the old section of the road at a cost of $20,000, and are spending $18,000 for the purchase of maintenance machinery. I want to know where that road is. Is it along the Bear river between the Mackenzie river and Great Bear lake?	_

the John R. MacNicol dam. No man has done more for the cause of water conservation-

Has provision been made for the control works at the south end of Okanagan lake, both in connection with repairs, if such are needed, and the keeping open of the channel of Okanagan river to take away the flood waters from the lake?

I am informed by my deputy that these works are taken care of under the general vote for harbours and rivers.

Supply-Public Works
Does that apply also to the renewing of the timbers on the protection breastwork at Penticton? That is a small breakwater erected for the purpose of providing shelter for boats on the lake.
I am not sure about that item.
I took the matter up with the minister earlier in the session, and I understood from a note I received that this was being taken care of. I presume it will be done out of the general vote.
I am told that if the hon. member received a letter from my department stating that we would proceed with it, we will do so.

Two other small breakwaters have been asked for at Peachland and Summerland. Okanagan lake, like all mountain lakes, is subject to sharp squalls coming on without notice, and the rough water created by such squalls makes it hazardous for boats. There has been a most interesting development in recent years, both for tourists and for residents, when they have been running a competition called the Okanagan fish derby in connection with which prizes are given for the biggest fish taken. It so happens that many of those large fish are taken on the west side of the lake in the vicinity of Peach-land and Summerland. The consequence is that if boats are fishing along that piece of exposed shore, and a sharp squall springs up, there is no place to which they can run for safety. This is a matter of great interest to all the inhabitants of the interior, because they come from there and from the south as well. Since the war the tourist business has increased and there are many boats on Okanagan lake. I am afraid we are going to have trouble if some assistance is not provided when these squalls come up. Furthermore, boats which are too large to be taken out of the water in the fall and are placed on chocks require some kind of breastwork to protect them from the winds which surge down the lake from the north. Something should be done in this case similar to what was done some years ago at Penticton.
Would this be a new work?
I think it would be.

I do not think we could use this vote for that purpose; it would require a special estimate. I am trying to recall if I have received any requests for these two projects.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the need of reconditioning the wharf at Seaton lake. I approached the department last April and was told that the district engineer had been instructed to examine the wharf and submit a report. Has the minister received the report of the engineer, and could some of this vote be devoted to reconditioning that wharf? I notice it is not mentioned specifically, and I wanted to be sure that some provision was made for it.

If it is an existing construction and the report received from the engineer warrants immediate repair, it will be undertaken under the general vote. I do not believe the report has been received concerning this project, but I shall look into it.
There is money for that purpose, provided that the engineer's report is favourable?

That will be enough.

Has the minister received a report on the project at Revelstoke which the department was looking into? This concerns the construction of a wing dam on the Columbia river to prevent the erosion of the bank some half a mile below Revelstoke. When I was last in touch with the department I was informed that they were awaiting the report of the engineer. In this connection f think it is appropriate for some member from British Columbia to pay a tribute to the work of Mr. Morton, the departmental engineer. I have heard nothing but the highest praise of that gentleman. I think he has far too much work to look after, with the staff at his disposal, and the result is that when we bring matters to the attention of the minister it takes too long for a report to be made. That is not Mr. Morton's fault, because there is more than he and his staff can do. I asked that the work on the dam at Revelstoke be undertaken before high water
Supply-Public Works

in order to prevent erosion, but as I understand it the investigation did not get under Way until the high water stage had been reached. I hope this work can be done before the next high water period. I hope also that the minister will consider giving his office in British Columbia the necessary staff to enable it to do the good work of which it is capable.

We lack staff in the engineers' branch, and I doubt if there is one of our offices which has not had men leave the service or go on superannuation. We are trying to replace these losses, but there seems to be a lack of engineering talent wishing to come into the government employ. We have made applications to the civil service commission to increase the staff.

Can the minister say anything about the work at Revelstoke? While I am on this subject I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West in connection with the dredging of the Arrow lake system, and to repeat my request for the replacement of the dredge on Shuswap lake. This is needed to do the work there and on the Thompson river. The dredge that is there now is some thirty years old, and is constantly in need of repair. This is quite a water system and there is an increasing amount of logging being done. Will the minister consider placing a new dredge there and getting the work under way as soon as possible, so that it may be completed before the next high water?

I nearly committed myself on Saturday to a new dredge on the Fraser river and on another river, and I do not know if I could commit myself to-day to another dredge on the Thompson river and one on the Columbia river. I understand that the life of a dredge is over forty years, and so if this one is only thirty years old, it should be good for another ten years.
It seems to need extensive repairs.
If it needs repairs, we will attend to them. As at Revelstoke, we are proceeding to have surveys made before the next high water period.
Is the vote for Bella Coola to cover the extension and repairs of the existing wharf?

It is to cover repairs and improvements to the actual wharf, the moving of the existing approach and float, the addition of a ICO by 200 feet wharf-head, and the construction of floats.
IMr. Fu'.tev..]

I have spoken to several of the oldest residents in this area about the condition of the existing wharf and its relationship to the river, which goes on the rampage quite often. The mouth is silting up, thus necessitating an extension to the wharf. I have been told that if the wharf were moved further out along the point, or even in the lee of the point it would1 provide shelter for the large fishing fleet which winters there. This would be better than to continue to extend 'the existing wharf and dabble with the river, because the whole mouth is filling up. When the tide goes out the whole fleet is left on the beach; the boats pile up on each other, and a lot of damage is done. I should like the minister to consider moving the wharf out farther. I think this could be worked out *between his engineers and the people in the locality.
An interesting development has taken place in recent years in the movement of cattle from the Williams lake country down the Bella Coola valley and thence on to Vancouver. However, the cattle men up in that country can do it at a more costly rate by taking them into Williams lake and shipping over the Pacific-Great Eastern when they land down in the Bella Coola valley they get their cattle all caught up in this mud flat where the silting takes place, and if a barge wharf were put in there they could load without any difficulty. The cattle coming in through the up-country via Bella Coola have plenty of natural feeding, and1 there is no cost to the cattlemen, whereas they have to buy feed when they ship out the other way. Several ranchers are actively interested in this, and>
if this facility were provided I am sure there would be more interest in shipping out by that route. At the same time this work going on in Bella Coola also affects Ocean Falls. As you know, that is a growing pulp and paper centre, and the people there suffer climate handicaps. It rains practically all the time.
Up British Columbia!

Well, I have to tell the truth once in a while, so help me. The only place where these people can have a real holiday and get out of the rain belt is Bella Coola, forty miles away. Yet when they go there to spend a holiday they run against this business of tying up their boats, and if there is a wind blowing the boat gets all smashed up. That is why it would be a benefit to the workers of Ocean Falls as well as to the people of Bella Coola.

Supply-Public Works
I have to 'bring to the minister's attention the extent to which these communities are dependent upon these wharves. Very often their whole livelihood depends on a decent float. Further to that, at one time $3,500 was voted for a float at Hunts Inlet; I. do not see it there now. The float was condemned a couple of years ago. There again is a fishing village which is completely isolated as regards getting to it or out of it, except for that float, and yet it is in such a condition that they cannot depend on it. Oona River is in the same position, and also Skidegate. The float at Skidegate is half sunk. As to getting lumber to build a float, I know I could scrounge enough off the beach to build one. So the material is right in the bay as far as building a float at Skidegate is concerned.
Speaking of the interior, there are quite a few independent loggers working along Babine Lake, and they have no wharf facilities. It would be in the interests of producing lumber if the department would heed the representations of the board of trade of Burns Lake and install that much-needed facility at the point.
I bring these various items to the attention of the minister not as a means of having money spent in the district, but rather to impress upon him the fact that these facilities, especially on the coast, are the only means of getting in and out of that area, and the fishermen whose whole capital is often tied up in one boat, are absolutely dependent upon decent facilities for tying up and landing. It is not a case of waiting until future years; the work should be done now, or there will be a menace and a serious handicap to the production of fish and the much-needed food which the world is demanding at the present time.
I leave these various matters in the hands of the minister, except that I should like to ask him one question: has the department considered the objections of the people of Port Essington to moving the float from Haysport to Tyee?
I am sorry that I could not get the information this afternoon, but the question will be noted and I will have the officials give that information to the hon. gentleman.

When I was home last winter they were complaining of the plans to move the float from Haysport to Tyee. The people of Port Essington did not want it moved, and a majority of the citizens signed a petition to that effect.

I want to compliment the minister on his staff in British Columbia, and particularly those who have worked in the Kootenay district, some of whom I have known for thirty years or more. They are efficient, hard-working and courteous, and the service they give is generally recognized by all people in the district regardless of political beliefs. I say this because I think that very often the services rendered by civil servants distant from Ottawa are not given sufficient recognition in Ottawa.
The people of my riding are pleased at the expenditures proposed in connection with the Arrow and Kootenay lakes; but I want to bring to the attention of the minister one or two matters connected with this vote. I speak for a riding which last year produced one hundred million dollars' worth of minerals, lumber and agricultural products, so it is a riding of some importance. I am not suggesting that the things which are desired by the people of the district can be done immediately, having regard to the shortage of material and of labour. But I do ask the minister and his department to give consideration to the provision of a very necessary float at Trail, in view of the increased navigation on the Columbia river. I am informed that during the last month or so we had more than forty boats come from Boulder dam and Spokane to the head of the lakes. There should also be extension and improvement to the present accommodation at Nakusp, Lardo and1 Nelson and when the time is ripe a float, built for St. Leon Hot Springs.
I do ask the minister to give some, consideration to these matters. Although we do not expect the work to be done while labour and materials are in short supply, we hope these projects wall be set on foot as soon as possible.

I am sorry I was not here on Saturday when the discussion took place with regard to Ripple Rock. I do not propose to go over the ground covered then, because according to Hansard there was a rather acrimonious debate.
Quite a ripple.

I believe the minister was under criticism in that regard. Usually we British Columbia members agree with one another, but in this case I commend the minister for closing down that work. He used excellent judgment when, he closed it down. As it is in my riding, I may say that I was a little nervous about going around that country because the people seemed to think I was the Minister of Public Works and was responsible for the work going on there. We have spent $800,000 there and have learned that the system that was being tried was entirely wrong. Ripple Rock will always be a great hazard. As a matter of fact, there are a great many marine hazards in British Columbia-Ripple Rock is not the only one -and it is interesting to note that during the war many thousands of ships, Russian, American and others, all strangers, went through there without one being wrecked on Ripple Rock. The only one that was wrecked was our own government Ship, and I think the captain or whoever was in charge would be the first to say that he committed an error in judgment when he got tangled up with the rock. The minister said that he had $1,900,000 available for its removal. I would like his assurance that he will start making that money available if someone comes along and offers a no-cure, no-pay proposition. Will he undertake that?
I would do a lot for my hon. friend, but I would not mingle in the Ripple Rock discussion. I see that my hon. friends are not all of one mind on the project.
We are all of one mind on the necessity for t'he work.
We all want it removed.

I hear one partisan saying that it cannot be done, and another that it should not be done. I do not think I should repeat what I said on Saturday; it would only start another long discussion. What I said, then was that the last estimate we received from the contractor was $1,900,000, and we tried to find out whether we could get a guarantee that he would execute the project for that price and give us an assurance that the work would be done.

Supply-Public Works
But that is what we could not get from any contractor, and we therefore decided not to proceed on that basis. As I explained on Saturday, we were sorry that we could not do the work under the present methods known to the department. I repeat, however, that we will continue to study the project and if any other method is found I think the government will be disposed to undertake these works. I do not say they will be done this year, or even next year. We do not want anybody to say that the officials of the department do not wish to go ahead with the work. There is nothing to that. We are ready to undertake it; it is a danger to navigation. Before we undertake the work, however, we want to have something definite as to price and completion of the work.
'Mr. PEARKES: It is not only a menace but a very serious hindrance to navigation, in that vessels have to tie up and wait for hours until the tide is favourable so that they can go by. The vessels that tie up, waiting for hours, losing valuable sailing time, need the removal just as much as the smaller vessels to which it is a danger.

I have here a report from the chairman of the board of directors of the national gallery. It states that in the home field the national gallery has had the most active year in its history. Six major channels of art education were vigorously employed with highly satisfactory results. In Ottawa special and regular exhibitions were held and these were attended by nearly 150,000 visitors; thirty lectures, attended by a total of more than 3,000 students and interested listeners were given.
The trustees continue to regard their work for other parts of Canada as of major importance. Loan exhibitions to points outside Ottawa were in greater demand than ever before and were sent out in larger numbers. The cumulative effect of these exhibitions is apparent in the steadily growing interest in art centres and increased attendance at individual galleries.
The distribution of good colour reproductions of Canadian paintings, whereby some of the benefits of the national gallery are carried to the remotest settlements has grown beyond the capacity of the present staff to cope with satisfactorily. Extra space and assistance must be provided if this useful work is not to be handicapped. During the year 163,210 prints were sent out, which is quadruple the number distributed last year, which in turn was double the total of the year before. The reproductions include the well-known silk-screen prints which are proving of inestimable value for school use.
The national gallery has originated a new plan to make the gallery more widely effective as an educational institution. With the cooperation of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a series of broadcasts to schools on outstanding Canadian artists was commenced last year. The broadcasts make use of the small colour prints issued by the national gallery, which are sent out in sets at a nominal price. Thus the school pupil or interested individual in any part of Canada
Supply-Public Works

can have before him a facsimile of the picture being discussed as he listens to the broadcast. Approximately 120,000 prints were requested last year and the demand for the coming year may reach half a million. The notebooks of pupils and reports submitted by schools have been excellent and indicate the far-reaching effects these broadcasts are having on pupil and parent alike. It is one of the most effective devices for making known to Canadians everywhere the work of our own artists and developing in. them an intelligent appreciation of art. As the technique of this method develops, the scheme can be extended to include other schools of art and other periods.
The total number of lectures and film showings given during the year in all parts of Canada was 267, an increase of 100 per cent over last year.
That the demand for what the art gallery can provide does not arise only from a limited number of interested enthusiasts but has its roots in all parts of the dominion and in all levels of society, is, indicative of an ever-increasing standard of education in Canada.
Under the direction of the national gallery, an exhibition called "What the art centre can do for your community" was developed and ten identical collections were prepared. These ten exhibitions are in continuous circulation throughout the country, even to the smaller and more remote towns, showing what can be done to make use of the facilities of the national gallery and other government sources. In addition to these collections, 138 loan exhibitions were circulated in all parts of Canada.

When they have not in stock what we need we have to buy from outsiders.

Does it mean that if, say the Department of National Defence has furniture in various temporary buildings, surplus as a result of the cutting down of services, that furniture has to be turned over to War Assets Corporation and resold to you?

Absolutely.
Supply-Public Works
And does the director of economies approve that? We have paid for that furniture once through national defence; do we have to pay for it again through this department?

Since the passing of the statute with respect to War Assets Corporation, they have disposed of any surplus in any department. Even the old salvage department under finance has been brought under that. Any surplus of any department is sent to War Assets corporation and is resold to public works if we need it, and we pay War Assets Corporation. We actually pay that corporation. For any goods they have sold they have to account, but we pay out of these votes.

The minister must be misinformed on that point, because during the discussion on War Assets Corporation at the previous session, or perhaps it was earlier this session, the same point was raised by some hon. member, and there was a special exception, which the government indicated was always evident, when one department of government was buying from another. I understood at that time, and I believe the house understood, that such material did not go to War Assets Corporation to be bought back by another department. I am quite sure we were so informed, but it might be a good time now to have the matter clarified in the interests of the position of War Assets Corporation as a distributor between departments.

I understand from my officials that we do purchase from War Assets corporation what they have on hand and what we need for different departments. Whether the actual transfer of funds is made or whether it is a matter of bookkeeping, I do not know. I cannot say.

I think the minister had better utilize the advice given him in this committee with respect to the purchase of new furniture to see that the policy of the govern-men in future is so orientated as to meet conditions as they should be met. We should not be buying new furniture at this time, with the tremendous amount of furniture bought by the various departments-and high-class furniture, too, according to the evidence brought before the committee and the house from time to time. If you buy through War Assets Corporation, this is what happens. Many of the departments are holding back lists of what they should disclose as surplus. In the meantime, while they are held back, we are buying new furniture out of current revenue or from the consolidated revenue fund. Later on, this

will be sent to War Assets Corporation; we shall have purchased new stuff in the meantime, and the other will go at second-hand prices to the public. The government, in exercising the kind of economy it should, ought to make a special survey of what there is in all the war departments, which were in some way integrated by a war economy system. We would not have to be buying furniture for ten or fifteen years if a proper survey were made to see what we have on hand. The minister knows there is a disposition in the departments to hold on to their furniture and other surplus assets until pressure is brought to bear. It is the old story again, that the government is not realizing that the war is over and that we are in an entirely different set of circumstances. These departments ought to be wound up, and such supplies should be used for the ordinary civil work of the government. I do not wish to be unduly critical of the minister, because he himself is not too sure of the propriety of the whole business and I am far less sure than he is.
If there is one thing more than another that the discussion of these estimates brings out, it is that the minister can say to his department and to all these wartime mushrooms-essential ones too-which have grown up: "After all, these things are not needed now". If he does not do something about the matter the opposition will swoop down on him again, and I suggest that he use this to see that economies are effected. He can use the opposition in having economies effected, because that is one of the jobs we are here for.

Taking 840,000,000 out of a total of $3,500,000,000, there is not much in the. way of economies that can be effected in my department. You are looking at small things in my department. Public works, acting as agents for other departments, goes first to War Assets Corporation and if they have on hand what we need we purchase from them. If they have not what we request, or what is asked for we, go outside. If a survey is to be made I do not think it will be made by public works, and I do not know what interference I can have with all these government departments. When they request a desk and a chair for a new office we have our man look into the matter, and the director of economy sees that it is needed, because the person who is coming in is not going to work standing up. When that is done I have to go ahead.

There may not be much standing done in some departments.

Perhaps not. We have to try to find a desk and chair. The Department of National Health and Welfare has doubled or trebled in the last two years. The Department of Veterans Affair is another department which has increased its work. When these departments ask for all this furniture I look around to War Assets Corporation and then to private enterprise to get it. It is all bought after tendering by well-known firms or by agreement. We cannot always get what we are looking for. I do not think I can bring about much economy under this item, because when a request comes in from a department it is approved by the official, a report is made and sent to the director who is appointed specially to scrutinize these requests. It then comes back with approval and is later sent to the treasury board after we have accepted it. I do not know how I can change the procedure; it is the regular procedure.

I would be content not to view this as a special criticism of the minister but rather as an indication to him of how the committee feels. If he will do his part in conveying to the proper quarters the remarks that he has heard to-day, and indicate to them that if this kind of thing is to continue these items will meet a forest fire of criticism at the next session, then I think we shall have done a job.

Perhaps the minister will accept a suggestion with a little humour and a lot of common sense. If the minister knows that furniture is required in one department, and that another department 'which is closing up has a surplus, and if he will transfer the furniture from one department to the other we would have economy in the assisting of the one and the closing down of the other.

All the information that we have received' has not as yet cleared up anything. The Minister of Public Works is in the unfortunate position of having other departments make requests of him. He indicates that he does not know whether they are justified. He does not understand the circumstances; he does not know how much is purchased from War Assets Corporation. He has not the information, and it is not his fault because he essentially is in the position of representing a department which is the cats-paw of all the others. In order to bring this matter to the attention of these people, and having regard to what the hon. member for Peel has said with respect to the surplus of furniture which one sees on every hand, and also with a view of showing the attitude of
the committee with respect to a' policy whereby one department of government sends back this surplus furniture to War Assets Corporation, and another department of government purchases it from that corporation, a most uneconomical system, I am going to move that item 600, amounting to $300,000 in the estimates for the year 1946-47, be reduced to $10. I do that because nothing has been indicated to support the necessity of it.

I do not know that I would admit everything which has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre. If hon. members wish to be fair to my department they could not reduce this amount to one dollar because up to date they have voted at least five-twelfths of it.
I am reducing this item.
Five-twelfths of the item has been voted.
I take issue with the minister on that.
Does the hon. member think that amount was not voted in interim supply?

No. I would say to the minister that when the interim supply bills were before the house and were passed the definite undertaking was given by the Minister of Finance that nothing that was done with respect to that vote would in any way place us in a worse position than- we were before the supply bills were passed in connection with the individual items. That undertaking stands. May I say to the minister that he is quite wrong i,n his assumption that the five-twelfths item applies to any one individual item, all of which are left to the discretion and the decision of the committee itself. I think everybody will understand that.

Perhaps my hon. friend is right. When we voted interim supply it was understood that it took away no rights that the committee possess to decrease the vote; but on the other hand we have to face this situation. Having had at my disposal five-twelfths of this amount to buy furniture requested by other departments, I have proceeded on that assumption and have purchased furniture. I do not know who will be held responsible for the meeting of those payments. I am giving the real facts, because on that assumption my officials assumed that we could dispose of the five-twelfths at least; and when requests came in in the ordinary course
Supply-Public Works

of business they probably proceeded and asked for tenders or bought from War Assets Corporation.
If I have no estimate at all to pay for the furniture the committee will realize that I am in one of those positions where the public service will not be efficiently carried on. If I am requested to buy furniture for veterans affairs or any other department I cannot buy it. .
Borrow, beg or steal from your neighbours.

I am trying to show what position I shall be in. I do not suppose the committee would accept the amendment, but if it did, on this item I would be in a quandary. I do not know whether I would be back in the house or whether I would be in the department looking to see where I could get the money, because I am sure I have expended -part of it. The hon. gentleman says that I have not proven that it is needed. Unless we change the whole set-up, how can I give any more information except to bring every file to the committee or answer any question which may be placed on the order paper or produce everything which we have done since March 31 of this year. When it is encumbered and we decide to purchase, it has to go to the treasury board and be approved.
If the hon. member wishes me to bring down every purchase we have made under this vote I can do so. But in all fairness to my department I do not think the amendment to bring it down to one dollar would meet the case. What the hon. member for Lake Centre has said, if he is trying to impress these departments as to the purchase of furniture, will reach the proper authorities. With this explanation I might ask the hon. member for Lake Centre to withdraw his amendment. It applies not only to the Department of Public Works, but to every other department of government, since the money is expended for all departments. In all fairness to those who have made these requests, 
which are justified, they cannot be deprived of the things they require to do the work given to them under the law.
